item: connecting() gives its shared library level back when its cleanup hits a MemoryError, and the swap's wait for the opens in flight re-checks every second
status: shipped (its own PR after #1429; this commit sits on the swap_window commit)
summary: The same instruction sweep as the swap window's, run on connecting()'s cleanup (the part that gives the shared level back), found the old shape `if _LOCK.shared_held_here() > before: _LOCK.release_shared()` (#1426's) leaving a level raised: the committed sweep, run on that module (c4882571f), lists 6 instructions that can allocate (the check's call and the getattr inside it, the release's call, the getattr and the subtraction inside it, and notify_all): 5 leave a level or the thread's record raised in the sweep's model (the small-integer subtraction makes no object, so 4 in that model where a call and an attribute fetch each count), and the sixth, notify_all, only loses the wake-up. The model is not the allocator: forced natively (warm and cold free lists, the old module and the new one) the old give-back fails only inside the `with self._lock:` of the release, its enter (the level stays raised) and, on cold free lists, its exit (the RLock stays owned), and the new give-back fails at the same two places, so for a MemoryError the one-call form changes nothing measured; it has one Python call fewer before the release (one interrupt site fewer), and the measurable gain is the record's initialiser below (the delta read of #1435's head, finding L-1). The counters are left out of the new sweep because a small-integer result is a cached object, pinned by a test. A level left raised makes every later swap_window (repair, restore, encrypt in place) refuse with LibraryBusy until restart: a named refusal of a rare operation, not a hang. Fixed: _Lock.release_shared_since(before) compares the thread's record with the value read BEFORE the take and gives the level back with no call between 'it is ours' and 'it is released'; the record is a thread-local that sets n in __init__ (at the thread's first read, which connecting() makes before it asks for a level): an attribute load, not a getattr call, and the first take replaces a value instead of making a dict entry (an allocation: forced with the allocator on cold free lists, the earlier class default left the count at 1 and the record at 0 at allocation 3, and the level raised until restart; the independent read of #1435's head, finding L1); the swap's own wait (exclusive) takes steps of _RECHECK_S, so the one call left after the level is back (notify_all) costs a lost wake-up one step and not the swap's deadline. tests/test_connecting_allocation_failures.py sweeps the cleanup (green; the swap that was already waiting must get through within 0.5 s), pins the release and the take structurally, and catches three mutants of the module's own source (the old pair of calls, a call before the release, a swap wait with no step). Residuals, named in connecting() and in the test: the CALL of release_shared_since itself, which no code after it can protect, and the exit of the `with self._lock:` inside it (it allocates when the tuple free list is empty and a failure leaves the lock held; see the swap_window row).
